property_summary: After lockInGuess is called with X wei, the caller's balance in C increases by exactly 0 or decreases by exactly X and C never holds more than expected so that sending >1 ether cannot increase the contract balance credited for the guess.

In the original contract, any call to lockInGuess that sends at least 1 ether always reverts if msg.value != 1 ether (i.e., only exactly 1 ether is accepted), so any successful call indicates msg.value == 1 ether; the mutant allows success when msg.value > 1 ether.
Calls to lockInGuess succeed (do not revert) only when the sent value equals exactly 1 ether.
Calls to lockInGuess revert if and only if the provided ether amount is not exactly 1 ether (so reverted == (amount != 1 ether)).

In the original contract, any call to lockInGuess that succeeds (does not revert) can only happen when the sent value is exactly 1 ether, so if a call succeeds then amount == 1 ether (mutant accepts >1 ether and breaks this).

After calling lockInGuess once from an address with 1 ether, that address's stored guess.block becomes nonzero (so a second lockInGuess call from the same address is rejected by the original but would be allowed by the mutant).

property_summary: lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) when the sender previously had no guess stored (i.e., their guess slot's block is zero).
Calling lockInGuess with msg.value == 1 ether should not revert when the caller has not previously locked a guess (i.e., first-time callers can successfully lock a guess).
Calling lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) for callers who have no prior guess stored (i.e., first-time callers) when sending exactly 1 ether.
Calling lockInGuess with value 1 ether should succeed (not revert) when the caller has not previously locked a guess, and should revert when the caller has previously locked a guess.

For any caller and any guess hash, if lockInGuess is called with a non-1 ether payment that reverts the require(msg.value == 1 ether), the reference contract leaves guesses[msg.sender].guess unset (default) while the mutant may have written the guess before the revert; therefore after a failing call the stored guess must remain bytes32(0) in the reference but can be non-zero in the mutant.

After any call to lockInGuess that supplies an incorrect payment (not 1 ether), the correct contract must not record the caller's guess (stored guess remains bytes32(0)); the mutant that writes the guess before checking payment can leave a non-zero stored guess after such a failing call.

For any caller and any hash, if lockInGuess is invoked with a payment different from 1 ether the reference contract never stores the caller's guess (stored guess remains bytes32(0)), whereas the mutant that writes the guess before checking msg.value can leave a non-zero stored guess after such a failing call.

For any caller and any guess hash, if lockInGuess is called with a payment that REVERTS (i.e. not exactly 1 ether) then the reference contract performs no state write for that caller (reads as bytes32(0) via the public mapping getter), whereas the mutant that writes the guess before checking msg.value may leave a non-zero stored guess after the failing call.

For any caller and any guess hash, if lockInGuess is invoked with a payment that reverts because msg.value != 1 ether, the reference contract leaves the stored guess for that caller as bytes32(0) (no state written), whereas the mutant that writes the guess before checking payment can leave a non-zero stored guess — so the reference always preserves bytes32(0) after a failing-payment call but the mutant can violate this.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether to the correct contract, the reference implementation records a nonzero future block number in guesses[msg.sender].block (so a subsequent public getter shows that block != 0), whereas the mutant that omits setting that block will leave the stored block equal to 0 for some caller — causing the property to fail.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract records a nonzero future block number for that caller (guesses[msg.sender].block != 0); the mutant that omits setting the block leaves it zero for some input, breaking this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always records a nonzero future block number in the caller's public guesses mapping (guesses(caller).block != 0); the mutant that omitted setting that field will leave it zero for some caller, violating this rule.

For any caller that successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract records a nonzero future block number in the caller's public guesses mapping (so the autogenerated getter guesses(address).block > 0 after the call); the mutant that omits writing that field leaves it zero for some callers, breaking this invariant.

For any caller who pays exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, the reference contract always sets the stored guesses(caller).block to a nonzero value (recording the future block); the mutant that omitted that assignment can leave guesses(caller).block equal to zero for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether when no prior guess exists, the reference contract always records a nonzero stored block number strictly greater than the current block (block.number) (because it stores block.number+1); the mutant that stores block.number can record a stored block equal to the current block, violating the rule for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the reference stores a nonzero guess-block strictly greater than the current block (block.number), whereas the mutant may store a guess-block equal to the current block, violating that strict > property for some input.

For any caller that successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether and no prior guess, the reference contract always records a stored block strictly greater than the current block (stores block.number+1), while the mutant may record a stored block equal to the current block (stores block.number), so the property is: after lockInGuess the stored block > block.number; the buggy version violates this for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the reference contract always records a stored guess-block strictly greater than the current block number (stores block.number+1); the mutant that stores block.number can record a stored block equal to the current block, violating the strict > relation for some inputs.

For any actor who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the reference contract records a stored block strictly greater than the current block number (stores block.number+1); the mutant that stores block.number can record a stored block equal to the current block, violating this strict-greater-than rule for some inputs.

After calling lockInGuess(hash) with 1 ether from any address that has no prior guess, the stored guesses(addr).block must be non-zero and strictly greater than block.number while guesses(addr).guess equals the provided hash; the mutant that swaps the two writes can transiently expose a state where block is set but guess remains zero during execution ordering leading to a different final state for some interleaving (fuzzed actor / hash) — specifically, the reference always ensures both fields reflect the inputs immediately after the call, while the mutant can be observed (by reading the public getter state) to have block set but guess not equal to the provided hash for some inputs when reordering interacts with how the EVM sequences storage writes and external reads in tests.

For any caller and any guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess call with exactly 1 ether from a fresh caller, the contract records both guesses[caller].block as nonzero and guesses[caller].guess equal to the provided hash; the mutant that swaps the two storage writes can be observed to leave guesses[caller].guess not equal to the provided hash for some inputs when interleaving/ordering differences are exploited.

For any caller and any bytes32 guess, after calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether from a fresh caller the contract records guesses[caller].block != 0 and guesses[caller].guess == provided guess; the mutant that swaps the two writes can leave guesses[caller].guess != provided guess for some inputs when an external reentrant/observer reads state between the two writes, so the property is violated by that mutant.

For any caller and any bytes32 guess, after calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether from a fresh caller the contract always records guesses[caller].block != 0 (nonzero) — the mutant that swaps the two writes can leave the stored block as set but cause the external call to observe inconsistent ordering leading to a failing observable state in some interleaving, so we assert that immediately after lockInGuess returns, the recorded block for the caller is nonzero (the reference satisfies this for all inputs; the mutant can fail for some inputs).

For any caller and any bytes32 hash, after a successful lockInGuess called with exactly 1 ether from that caller, the contract's public auto-generated getter for guesses(caller).guess equals the provided hash; the mutant that swaps the two storage writes can be observed (via a reentrant attacker) to leave guess not equal to the provided hash for some inputs.

Reference ensures settle cannot be executed in the same block as lockInGuess (require block.number > recorded), so after lockInGuess the contract balance cannot be drained by immediately calling settle in same block; the mutant allowing >= lets an attacker call settle in same block and withdraw funds — the property: for any addr that just locked a guess this block, calling settle in the same block does not succeed on the reference but can succeed on the mutant for some inputs.

For any address that locks a guess in block N, attempting to call settle in the same block must fail on the reference (require block.number > recorded) — the mutant allowing >= lets settle succeed in the same block in some cases, letting the caller withdraw funds immediately.

For any caller who just locked a guess in block N, calling settle in the same block must revert (reference requires block.number > N), whereas the mutant (using >=) can allow settle to proceed in the same block for some inputs, enabling a successful withdrawal; the test fuzzes the guess and actor to find such a case.

For any caller that locks a guess at block N, attempting to call settle in the same block must not succeed (settle should not transfer funds / should effectively be no-op or revert); the mutant changing '>' to '>=' allows settle to run in the same block and can succeed for some guesses, violating this rule.

For any caller and any guess, if they lock in a guess in block N then attempting to run settle in the same block must not succeed on the reference (settle must not return success / transfer), whereas the mutant allowing '>=' can permit settle to proceed (and possibly pay out) in the same block for some fuzzed guesses/inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess and then calls settle, the reference contract always clears their stored guesses[msg.sender].block to 0 by the end of settle (so address(c).balance decreases by 2 ether only when block cleared), while the mutant that clears the block after the transfer can leave guesses[msg.sender].block non-zero when the transfer to a malicious/ revert-causing recipient fails during the transfer, causing observable difference in behavior.

After any call to settle by a player who previously locked a guess, the reference contract always clears guesses[player].block to 0 regardless of whether transferring payout succeeds, whereas the mutant (which clears the block only after attempting transfer) can leave guesses[player].block non-zero if the transfer to a reverting recipient fails.

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 in the reference implementation; the mutant that clears the block only after a potential transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero if the transfer to the caller reverts, violating this rule.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle, the correct contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 by the end of the call; the mutant that clears the block only after attempting a transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the transfer to the caller reverts.

For every caller who previously locked in a guess, after calling settle the reference contract always resets guesses[caller].block to 0 (even if the payout transfer to caller reverts), whereas the mutant that only clears the block after the transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the recipient's fallback reverts.

For any caller who locked a guess hashed against the future blockhash, calling settle after that block either (in the correct contract) only succeeds in paying out when the stored guess equals keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)) — i.e., the stored guess never equals keccak256(storedBlock) for all possible storedBlock values, so the contract never erroneously pays out when guesses are meant to match blockhash-based answer; the mutant replaces blockhash with the plain block number allowing some fuzzed guesses to match keccak256(storedBlock) and thus wrongly trigger a payout.

For every lockInGuess and settle sequence the reference contract never pays out because a guess matching keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)) is infeasible for arbitrary storedBlock values, whereas the mutant that uses keccak256(storedBlock) can be met by some fuzzed guess and thus will sometimes increase the contract balance (i.e., cause a payout).

For any attacker-provided guess and booked block number, the reference contract C never considers the guess equal to keccak256(abi.encodePacked(blockhash(bookedBlock))) for any bookedBlock (so settle never pays out), whereas the mutant can consider a guess equal to keccak256(abi.encodePacked(bookedBlock)) for some fuzzed guess and bookedBlock, causing a payout; we assert that settle never transfers funds from the contract for all fuzzed inputs on the reference but can on the mutant.

For any attacker guess and timing, the reference contract never pays out funds on settle (address(c).balance never decreases after settle), whereas the mutant can sometimes treat a stored block number as the answer and thus pay out (decreasing address(c).balance) for some fuzzed inputs.

For any fuzzed stored guess and booked block set by lockInGuess, the reference C never considers the guess equal to keccak256(abi.encodePacked(blockhash(bookedBlock))) (so settle will not report a successful match immediately when called from the next block), whereas the mutant that hashes the raw block number can make the stored guess equal that value for some fuzzed inputs causing settle to appear successful (i.e. the mutant can make settle return true while the reference always returns false for the same admissible inputs).

For any caller who locked a guess and the block has advanced, calling settle on the correct contract will never reduce the contract balance below 1 ether (it only pays out when it has >=2 ether), whereas the mutant can pay out 2 ether even when its balance is only 1 ether, causing address(c).balance to drop below 1 ether for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the locked block, the correct contract never allows its balance to decrease below 1 ether (it only transfers 2 ether when it holds >= 2 ether), whereas the mutant can transfer 2 ether even when its balance is exactly 1 ether, making address(c).balance < 1 ether after settle for some inputs.

For every admissible input, after a successful settle call the reference contract never lets its balance drop below 1 ether (it only pays out when it has >= 2 ether); the mutant can violate this by allowing a 2-ether payout when the contract balance is only 1 ether, making address(c).balance < 1 ether for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the locked block, the reference contract will never revert during the payout attempt (i.e., calling settle will succeed or fail only due to guess mismatch) when the contract has at least 1 ether upfront provided by the test runner; the mutant can cause settle to revert when it attempts to transfer 2 ether while only 1 ether exists because it relaxes the balance check, leading to a revert for some fuzzed inputs.
